# Manifold mailbox — the retry loop that spends a rationed resource

**Status: r1.9, authored at Waffles' seat 2026-08-05 ~04:50Z, off a LIVE
OUTAGE. Tom's estate refused to boot at 04:28Z and stayed down. Every
number below was read from the estate's own bytes before anything was
touched. Nothing in this brief is inferred from a symptom.**

## What happened, in one paragraph

Tom stopped the estate with Ctrl-C. The kernel wrote its own shutdown report
addressed to the estate's status record (`#manifold.kernel`), but the carrier
for that record is the spine — one of the seats the same shutdown was tearing
down. The report could not be delivered, the mailbox is built never to lose a
record, and it re-presented the bytes in an unbounded loop: reconnect,
re-attach at generation+1, present, link dies, repeat. Each iteration spends
one `ProvenanceParticipant` slot. Sixty-four of those exist per participant and
they refill over two hours. The loop consumed all 64 in 118 seconds. On the
next boot the kernel could not take its own seat and refused to start, because
a kernel that cannot say what is running is running blind (KERNEL-BRIEF R6).

**The estate was healthy the entire time it ran.** This is a shutdown-path
defect reachable by an ordinary Ctrl-C, which means it has been available on
every estate stop ever performed.

## The measured evidence

Boot refusal, verbatim from Tom's terminal:

    ReceiptCapacityExceeded(CredentialAttach {
      participant_id: 0, capability_generation: Generation(76),
      scope: ProvenanceParticipant, limit: 64, occupied: 64 })

Two seats on conversation 7 in `.manifold/mailbox/manifold.kernel/`:

| seat | participant | generation | credential written |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a434dc9c…` | 1 | **10** | 2026-08-05T02:19:48Z (the boot) |
| `ba6d3199…` | 0 | **76** | 2026-08-05T04:30:45Z |

`pending-record.json` on seat `ba6d3199…`, 14,578 bytes:

- `staged_under_generation: 12`
- `staged_at: 2026-08-05T04:28:47.891266Z`
- `unanswered_presentation: Issued`
- payload decodes to `{"version":2,"from":"kernel",…}` whose body is
  `{"v":1,"occasion":"shutdown","kernel_pid":86656,…}`

Generation 12 → 76 is **64 attaches inside 118 seconds** — one every 1.84 s.

Participant 1 sat at generation 10, untouched, from the 12:19 boot through
shutdown. **There was no drip during the run.** The entire burn is in the
shutdown/restart window.

## Root cause — the backoff is on the wrong loop

`crates/manifold-node/src/mailbox/driver/submit.rs`, `MailboxSubmit::admit`:

```rust
loop {
    match self.admit_once(&payload).next(earlier.clone()) {
        Next::Record(seq)          => { … return …; }
        Next::Represent(error)     => { self.report_link_lost_under_admission(…);
                                        self.reconnect()?; }
        Next::Keep(..) | Next::Clear(..) => return Err(error),
    }
}
```

`Next::Represent` retries **forever**: no attempt bound, no delay, nothing in
the loop body between one presentation and the next but a reconnect.

`crates/manifold-node/src/mailbox/driver/attach.rs:191`, `reconnect()`, does
`let mut backoff = Backoff::new();` — **constructed fresh on every call** — and
prints "waiting for it as long as it takes, up to {MAX_BACKOFF} between
attempts".

The attach succeeded on attempt 1 every single time ("re-attached … on attempt
1 as participant 0 (generation 76)"). So the backoff never advanced past its
first step, and was discarded at the end of each call regardless.

⇒ **The advertised 60-second ceiling governs the loop that is not repeating,
and does not exist on the loop that is.** The operator reads a message
promising a slow retry while the process spins at half-second intervals.

`admission_token` is rebuilt from the *current* generation on each pass, so
retries are correctly not replays. The token domain moving is by design. What
is not by design is that moving it costs a rationed slot.

## The class this belongs to

Two designs, each defensible in isolation:

1. *the mailbox never loses a record — retry until it gets through*
2. *a participant may hold 64 provenance fingerprints, refilling over 2 hours*

**Nothing anywhere holds both facts at once.** One spends without limit what the
other rations. Neither component is wrong on its own terms and the failure is
invisible to any test that exercises either one alone.

**Rule to carry forward: a retry loop must know the cost of an attempt.** If an
attempt consumes a bounded resource, the loop owns a budget, not just a delay.

The capacity cap is the only component that behaved well here — it converted an
unbounded loop into a loud, bounded refusal. **It must not be raised.** Raising
it converts a two-hour outage into a longer one at a larger number.

## The client's classification is CORRECT — read at my bytes, r1.6

Before commissioning R2/R3 I checked whether manifold's `admit` would even
*honour* a typed refusal, or whether fixing the server would leave the loop
spinning anyway. **It honours it.** `Presented::next` in `submit.rs:155` is a
total mapping and its own doc says so — *"a total mapping, so the rule 'only a
known fate spends the staged bytes' is one function and can be checked without
a broker"*:

    Self::Settled(error) => match earlier {
        Some(p) => Next::Keep(Kept::EarlierPresentationUnanswered(p), error),
        None    => Next::Clear(Spent::DidNotCommit, error),
    },
    Self::Unknown(error) =>
        if is_transport_failure(&error) { Next::Represent(error) }
        else { Next::Keep(Kept::ThisPresentationUnanswered, error) },

`Keep` and `Clear` both **return** out of the loop. **`Represent` — the looping
arm — is reachable only when the failure classifies as a TRANSPORT failure.**

⇒ Two consequences, and both matter for how this work is scoped.

1. **R4 alone stops this loop — CONDITIONAL, see r1.7 below.** A
   `StaleAuthority::Live` *that arrives* comes in as `Settled`; our record
   carried `unanswered_presentation: Issued`, so `earlier` is `Some`, so it
   routes to `Keep` — bytes retained, operator told, loop over. No client change
   is needed to make the mapping land. **The conditional is entirely on the
   word ARRIVES**, which is liminal's side of the boundary.
2. **The client was never sloppy.** It looped because a socket closed mid-frame,
   which is a transport failure by every test available to it — and *waiting as
   long as it takes* is the correct response to a transport failure. **The
   client did the right thing with the only information it was given.** The
   defect is that the information was wrong, and that the cost of waiting was
   invisible.

### r1.7 — A BEST-EFFORT REFUSAL CAN REPRODUCE THE BUG THROUGH THE FIX

**Hermes, 04:54Z, mid-build, sent as a constraint to the implementer.** There
are two ways to put a refusal on this wire and they are not equivalent:

- **`FrameAction::Respond`** enqueues the frame and **propagates an enqueue
  failure as a real error**. The connection stays open.
- **`FrameAction::RespondThenClose`** is **BEST-EFFORT**, and the code says so
  itself (`process.rs` ~960-985): *"a failed enqueue here is logged and
  swallowed, NEVER PROPAGATED … The single best-effort drain happens on the
  `ProcessStatus::Close` path in `service_socket`, so NO WRITE IS FORCED (OR
  AWAITED) here."*

⇒ **If the mapped refusal goes out via `RespondThenClose` and the enqueue fails,
or the unawaited drain does not flush, the client sees a closed socket with no
frame — bit-for-bit the signature it already reads as transport failure.**
`is_transport_failure` says yes, `Presented::next` routes to `Represent`, and
the loop resumes **with the fix installed, the brief closed, and everyone
believing it landed.** It would fail to fix precisely under load, which is
exactly when it matters.

**And the obvious guard cannot see it.** A test asserting *"not `Fatal`"* passes
either way — `RespondThenClose` is not `Fatal`. That is the circularity problem
one layer further out than the one already caught: **the failure and the success
produce the same observable at the seam where we were planning to look.**

*Added to R4 acceptance:* the assertion must distinguish **a response that keeps
the connection OPEN**, not merely a non-`Fatal` outcome. And if the verify stage
cannot use the ordinary `Respond` path where the lookup stage can, the
implementer must **STOP AND REPORT rather than fall back**.

**The generalisation worth carrying past this fix: a best-effort refusal is a
contradiction.** A refusal exists in order to inform; one that may not arrive is
a refusal that may not refuse. `RespondThenClose` is therefore never the right
vehicle for a refusal whose whole purpose is to stop a client retrying.

### r1.8 — the auth gate: FOUND, and it is an instance of the hazard

I raised this as REPORTED at 04:58Z, unread, on the grounds that the one place
we pointed at and said *"look, it already works"* was described in exactly the
words that would make it not work. **Hermes read it. It is
`RespondThenClose`, in both arms** (`apply.rs`, `connect_response`): auth token
rejected ~362, version negotiation failure ~373. And `process.rs` names it
inside the best-effort comment — *"(a `ConnectError` from the auth gate)"* — so
the auth gate is not merely *a* user of that path, **it is the case the
best-effort machinery was written for.**

**His own precedent argument loses half its weight and he struck it himself.**
The two exemplars offered for "the capability already exists" are not equal:

- **The auth gate** proves only that *inform-then-close* exists. It does **not**
  prove a *reliable refusal* exists. It moves out of the argument as an exemplar
  and back in as a finding.
- **The lookup-stage `StaleAuthority`** (`ops_attach_lookup.rs`) is the
  load-bearing one — an ordinary `Respond`, enqueue failure propagated,
  connection open. **That is the exemplar R4 must match**, and the only one that
  carries the claim. The two-stage sentence survives intact.

**Blast radius, scoped — it is NOT ours.** These are connect-time refusals,
before participant capability is negotiated and before any attach. A dropped
`ConnectError` burns **no** `ProvenanceParticipant` slots and **bricks no
estate**; the receipt-cap consequence is entirely absent. What survives is the
loop shape.

**The sharper arm is version negotiation: a client that must upgrade to proceed
never learns that it must.** No amount of retrying can ever fix that — it is an
infinite loop against a *permanent* condition.

⇒ **And that names what silence actually costs, which is more than the reason.**
A retry policy is a function of expected DURATION. "Wait as long as it takes" is
correct for transport failure only because transport failures are presumed
transient. **A bare close asserts transience.** So silence does not merely
withhold *why* — it misclassifies *whether this will ever change*, and the
client then applies a policy that is correct for the failure it was told about
and wrong for the one that happened.

⇒ **Note the inversion about the cap.** Our incident terminated after 118
seconds because a rationed resource ran out and refused loudly. **The auth-gate
case has no such terminator** — nothing is rationed at connect time, so the loop
has nothing to stop it. The receipt cap did not merely limit the damage in our
case; it is the reason ours was survivable at all, and its absence elsewhere is
why the same shape is worse there despite the smaller blast radius.

⚠ **FREQUENCY IS UNCLAIMED, by both of us.** Neither has evidence about how
often an enqueue fails or the unawaited drain misses. **The hazard is structural
and the structure is proven; no instance has been observed.** Our own incident
is not evidence for it either — ours died at `Fatal`/`Close`, which sends
nothing by design and never reaches the best-effort path at all.

**Owner: liminal, raised as its own item, not folded into #11** — different
operation, different stage, no shared code path with the attach case. Folding it
would hide that it is reachable by anyone who ever gets a token wrong or runs an
old client.

So R2 and R3 are **not** the fix for this incident; R4 is. R2 and R3 are
defence-in-depth for the case where the failure genuinely *is* transport — a
broker that is really down, really unreachable, for a really long time — where
"as long as it takes" is right in principle and still spends 64 rationed slots
at 1.84-second intervals. That case is untouched by anything liminal does.

## The repair — three requirements

**R1 — the kernel says goodbye before it kills the postman.**
The shutdown report must be published *before* teardown begins, while the spine
is still serving; or, if the report cannot be published, the kernel must say so
and proceed rather than stage it for a carrier it is about to destroy. Staging
a record addressed to a subsystem the same operation is dismantling is the
defect, and it is an ordering defect, not a delivery one.
*Acceptance:* a clean stop publishes the shutdown report with the spine live
and leaves **no** `pending-record.json` behind. Red-first: a test that stops
the estate and asserts the staging file is absent must fail before the fix.

**R2 — the brake goes on the loop that repeats.**
The backoff belongs to `admit`'s retry cycle, not to a single `reconnect` call
that resets it. Either hoist a `Backoff` to the `admit` loop and advance it on
every `Next::Represent`, or thread the caller's backoff into `reconnect` so it
survives across attempts.
*Acceptance:* a fixture whose presentation always fails and whose attach always
succeeds shows delays advancing toward `MAX_BACKOFF` across iterations. Today
that fixture produces a flat, immediate spin — it is the red proof and it must
be committed.

> ⚠ **R2 MUST NOT LAND WITHOUT R3, AND HERE IS THE ARITHMETIC.** Hermes's r1.9
> finding is that the receipt cap detected this loop **only because its TTL
> exceeds the retry interval** — slots pile up faster than they age out. State
> it exactly: with retry interval `T` and provenance TTL `L`, live slots settle
> at `L/T`, so the detector fires only while `T ≤ L/64`.
>
> `L` = 7 200 s ⇒ **the detector works only while the retry interval stays under
> 112.5 s.**
>
> - Today `T` ≈ **1.84 s** — margin **61×**.
> - **After R2**, `T` rises to `MAX_BACKOFF` = **60 s** — margin **1.875×**.
>
> **Our own repair cuts the safety margin from sixty-one-fold to under two-fold.**
> A `MAX_BACKOFF` of two minutes instead of one — a change anyone might make for
> unrelated reasons — would take the detector below the line and it would never
> fire again, silently. **R2 in isolation degrades the only thing that ended
> this incident.**
>
> R3 is what makes that safe: it replaces an *accidental* bound (a rationed
> resource happening to run out) with an *intentional* one (the loop counting its
> own budget). **So R3 is not defence-in-depth behind R2 — it is R2's
> precondition.** Land R3 first or land them together; never R2 alone.

**R3 — the retry knows what an attempt costs.**
`admit` must carry an attempt budget derived from the attach capacity it spends,
and on exhausting it must fail LOUDLY with the record left staged and a message
naming the resource, the count, and the refill window — never silently, and never
by continuing. The operator must learn "I have spent 64 of 64 attach slots and
they refill over two hours" from the process that spent them, at the time it
spends them, not from a refusal to boot two minutes later.
*Acceptance:* the exhaustion message names the scope, the limit, the observed
occupancy and the time the first slot frees.

### r1.3 — THE FIX IS A MAPPING, NOT A DESIGN. The wire already carries it.

**Amendment 2026-08-05 ~04:45Z, Hermes Crumpet, and it shrinks the repair
dramatically.** He went looking for whether a typed attach refusal is even
representable on the wire, expecting the answer to be no and the fix to need a
new `ServerValue` plus a version bump. **It is already there:**

    StaleAuthority::Live {
        request: CommonStaleAuthorityEnvelope::CredentialAttach(..),
        current_generation: Generation,
    }

That is exactly the answer the mailbox needed — not "something went wrong" but
**"your authority is stale, the live generation is N"**. A client told that can
classify it as terminal for the credential it holds and stop. The envelope
enumerates `CredentialAttach` as its first variant and the codec maps it back to
`ClientDiscriminant::CredentialAttachRequest`, so the round trip is complete and
tested.

**And the server already sends it — in the same operation.**
`ops_attach_lookup.rs:207`:

    CredentialAttachLookupResult::StaleAuthority(_) =>
        CredentialAttachResponse::stale_authority(envelope, slot.member.generation())

⇒ **CREDENTIAL ATTACH HAS TWO STAGES, LOOKUP AND VERIFY. BOTH CAN FAIL ON A
STALE GENERATION. THE LOOKUP STAGE ANSWERS THE CLIENT WITH THE CURRENT
GENERATION. THE VERIFY STAGE HANGS UP.** Same operation, same failure class,
same connection, two stages, opposite behaviour — and the one that hangs up is
the one that fired.

The plumbing, the wire type, the codec, the discriminant and a working call site
all exist. Nobody has to invent a refusal or negotiate a version.

**The partition now has a concrete first member and a mechanical test.**
`AttachVerificationError` is a 12-variant enum: `Conversation`, `Participant`,
`Generation`, `Secret`, `BindingState`, `MarkerProof`, `RecoveryAuthority`,
`PendingTerminalSequence`, `ResultBinding`, `ResultGeneration`,
`LifecycleOrder`, `TerminalHistory`. **Every one describes something the CLIENT
presented. Not one describes an impossible server state.** So both `map_err`
sites in `ops_attach_verify.rs` are unambiguously refusals-wearing-an-
invariant's-coat, and the enum was already doing the classification work before
the `format!` threw it away. `Generation` — *"Request generation is not the
current live generation"* — is this incident's signed-under-12-presented-
under-76, named in the protocol crate an hour before it took the estate down.

**The partition test (Hermes's, adopted): look at the ERROR TYPE being
converted, not the call site.** If its variants name things the *client* did, it
is a refusal and the conversion is a downgrade. If its variants name states the
*server* cannot be in, it is a true invariant and closing is honest. Mechanical
enough to run over all 266 without adjudicating each one, and it puts the burden
on a type that already exists rather than on a reviewer's judgement.

**The generator is larger than this path.** Hermes counted **266
`StateError::invariant` sites** in the participant production path; every one
of them, if reached, is a silent connection close. Most are genuine invariants
where no truthful response exists and closing is right — the claim is not that
all 266 are wrong. The *class* is "protocol-legible refusal converted to an
opaque internal error", and this incident proves at least one member of it is
both reachable and catastrophic. Raised as his #11, no longer parked. He notes
the identical shape one layer down: haematite destroys a tree error's type at a
catch-all in `db/helpers.rs`, which is why liminal can never discriminate it —
a defect he had recorded as someone else's and then shipped himself.

**What this changes for R1.** Since the presentation *was* refusable and the
server merely failed to say so, the kernel is **not** obliged to solve this by
never publishing a goodbye. A client that receives a typed terminal refusal
stops on its own. R1 remains right and worth doing; it is no longer the only
thing standing between an ordinary Ctrl-C and a dead estate.

**STILL REPORTED, NOT FOUND:** *which* arm fired. It does not change the
client-side symptom — every failure arm in that function terminates in the same
silent close — but the specific reason is unknown until someone reads the
server's own log line. `tracing::warn!(%error, "participant request failed
closed")` fires on exactly that path and `{error:?}` carries the original typed
refusal inside the string, so the answer was in the estate's stdout for
04:28:47–04:30:45Z. No log file exists on disk — **the estate logs to the

**CLOSED UNKNOWABLE, 04:44Z.** Tom checked; it is not recoverable. The arm that
fired is permanently unknown for this incident and is recorded as a gap rather

**That perishability is itself a finding.** The single line naming *why* the
